whyEn: Communication looks unexaminable until you see how this chapter is built: it is all named techniques and classifiable question types — open-ended versus closed versus payoff questions, active listening, the six rescue strategies (facilitate, be quiet, clarify, redirect, interpret, simplify), the six named interviewing errors, and a gesture-by-gesture cross-cultural table that writes its own matching questions. It also hides a clinical instrument: the introduce-and-ask-the-name opening that doubles as a one-second mini mental status exam screening six pairs of cranial nerves. On the BC practical side this chapter is worth real percentage points — communication with patient, partner, and bystanders is an explicit deduction category on every simulation. One thorough pass to learn the taxonomies, then drill the confusable pairs.
whyZh: 沟通看似没法考，直到你看清这一章的构造：全是有名有姓的技巧和可分类的题材——开放式、封闭式与高回报提问的三分法，积极倾听，问诊救场六招（促谈、留白、澄清、拉回、试解、化简），六种被点名的问诊错误，还有一张逐个手势列出的跨文化对照表，天生就是配对题。它还藏着一件临床仪器：自我介绍加问名字的开场，同时是一次1秒内完成、筛查六对脑神经的微型精神状态检查。在BC实操考里，这章值的是实打实的百分点——与患者、搭档、旁观者的沟通是每个模拟站明码标价的扣分项。认真过一遍学会分类法，再专攻易混对。

sections.titleEn: Internal Factors: The Attitude the Patient Reads Instantly
sections.titleZh: 内在因素：患者一眼就能读出的态度

points.en: The chapter's premise: patients are not medical puzzles, nuisances, or interruptions — they are the reason paramedics exist, and the S in EMS stands for service. Seeing people only as their medical problems is named as the shallow approach to prehospital care.
points.zh: 本章的前提：患者不是待解的医学谜题，不是麻烦，更不是打扰——他们是救护员这份职业存在的理由，EMS 里的 S 就是服务（service）。把人只看成『他的病』，被原书点名为院前急救的浅薄做法。

points.en: Genuinely liking people is an entry requirement, not a nicety: patients and families detect a false attitude in the blink of an eye, and the paramedic who does not like people ends up delivering marginal care and having a short career. Tolerating body fluids on your uniform without a syllable of protest is part of the deal.
points.zh: 真心喜欢与人打交道是入行门槛，不是加分项：患者和家属眨眼之间就能识破虚假的态度；不喜欢人的救护员，最终给出的只会是勉强及格的照护，职业生涯也长不了。制服被弄脏时一个字的抱怨都不能有——这本来就是这份工作的一部分。

points.en: At least half of a paramedic's calls go inside people's homes, day and night, at the most private moments of their lives. The chapter's reframe: treat every invitation into a home as a personal honour — you are welcome at births and deaths where no one else would be — and the career becomes fulfilling instead of drudgery.
points.zh: 救护员至少一半的出勤要走进别人家里，不分昼夜，撞见的都是人家最私密的时刻。原书给的心态调法：把每一次被请进家门都当作个人的荣幸——在出生与死亡这种旁人一概不得入内的时刻，你被允许在场——这样职业才是滋养而不是苦役。

points.en: Multitasking here means emotional bandwidth: while kneeling in front of the symptom-denying patient, you must simultaneously register the terrified spouse beside him — and feel something for both. That dual awareness is a defining gift of health care providers.
points.zh: 这里说的『一心多用』指情感带宽：跪在那个嘴上否认症状的患者面前时，你必须同时看见他身旁吓坏了的配偶——并且对两个人都有真实的共情。这种双线觉察正是医疗照护者的天赋所在。

sections.titleEn: External Factors: Look the Part, Control the Scene, Actually Listen
sections.titleZh: 外在因素：形象到位、控住现场、真的在听

points.en: Professional appearance is a communication tool: a clean, pressed uniform, a name and certification level others can read easily, and etiquette that inspires respect in strangers all buy patient confidence before a word is spoken.
points.zh: 职业形象本身就是沟通工具：干净熨帖的制服、旁人一眼能读到的姓名和执业级别、能赢得陌生人敬意的职业礼仪——话还没出口，患者的信心就已经被这些买到手了。

points.en: Communication is defined as transmitting information to another person, and for paramedics it runs on two channels — verbal and body language. Listening is itself communication, because it transmits information too.
points.zh: 沟通的定义是向另一个人传递信息，对救护员来说走两条通道——言语和肢体语言。倾听本身也是沟通，因为倾听同样在传递信息。

points.en: Active listening — the technique nearly all professional interviewers use — means repeating the key parts of the patient's answers back to them, ideally while taking notes. It convinces patients you want to hear them, and it confirms the information so nothing is misunderstood.
points.zh: 积极倾听——几乎所有职业访谈者的常规手法——就是把患者回答里的关键内容复述回去，最好同时做记录。它让患者相信你真想听，也把信息核对了一遍，杜绝误解。

points.en: Three named sins of inattention: treating patients like nuisances, talking about someone in their presence as if they were an object or absent, and asking a question you will repeat later because you did not attend to the first answer — write answers down instead.
points.zh: 被点名的三宗『不专心之罪』：把患者当麻烦；当着本人的面谈论他、仿佛他是件物品甚至不存在；以及问过的问题因为没认真听回答而稍后再问一遍——正确做法是当场记下来。

points.en: Scripted courtesies with rationale: answer thanks with 'You are very welcome!' — never 'No problem', which implies the patient was almost a nuisance; when a patient apologizes for incontinence, vomiting, or needing to be carried, the reply is that this is what we do, and we are here because we want to be.
points.zh: 带理由的礼貌话术：患者道谢时回『不客气，应该的！』——绝不说『没事儿』，那话外音是『你还不算太麻烦』；患者因失禁、呕吐或需要被抬下楼而道歉时，回答是：不用抱歉，这就是我们的工作，我们是自愿来的。

points.en: Noise doctrine: shouting is contagious and excites the whole scene, so do not shout. In a bar, recruit the bartender — music off, lights up, an eye on the patrons — and move the patient out fast, ideally to the back of the ambulance; shut down compressors and noisy diesels as soon as possible; and speak close to the patient's ear in a calm voice, which signals your emotions are under control and helps the patient stay calm.
points.zh: 噪音法则：喊叫会传染并让全场兴奋起来，所以不要喊。在酒吧出勤就借力酒保——关音乐、开大灯、盯着其他客人——并尽快把患者转移出去，最好转到救护车厢里；压缩机和轰鸣的柴油机能关就早关；凑近患者耳边用平稳的声音说话，这既表明你情绪在控，也帮患者稳住。

points.en: Take the history in one organized pass — it keeps you structured and makes people take the questions seriously. Personal questions need a managed scene: ask them quietly and in private, because even a trusting patient will not discuss some things in front of others. And remember the payoff questions — items outside routine history that repeatedly deliver information critical to the presumptive diagnosis.
points.zh: 病史要一次性、成体系地问完——你自己有条理，患者也会认真对待你的问题。私密问题则要先经营好现场：安静、无旁人时再问，因为再信任你的患者，有些事也不肯当众讲。另外别忘了『高回报问题』——那些不属于常规病史、却一再换回对拟诊断至关重要信息的提问。

points.en: In chaotic, noisy, even dangerous environments, the job is to build a safe zone around the patient — shut out everything else and focus on this one person, because calm is part of the medicine.
points.zh: 在混乱、嘈杂甚至危险的环境里，任务是给患者围出一个安全区——把其他一切隔在外面，只专注眼前这一个人，因为『让人安静下来』本身就是治疗的一部分。

sections.titleEn: Developing Rapport: Name, Voice, Fear, Pain, Modesty, No Judging
sections.titleZh: 建立融洽关系：名字、声音、恐惧、疼痛、体面、不做法官

points.en: People in crisis are highly perceptive — no pretence survives a patient's bedside. The core challenge of the therapeutic communicator: convey calm, unmistakable, genuine concern for someone you have never met, so the patient's fear eases and their own internal healing power can be harnessed.
points.zh: 身处危机的人感知力惊人——任何伪装到了床边都会被拆穿。治疗性沟通者的核心课题是：向一个素不相识的人传递出平静、清晰、真诚的关切，让恐惧退场，把患者自身的自愈力量调动起来。

points.en: Inflection carries as much as words: use the calm, steady tone of someone who cares for you when you are hurt — the voice itself is a reassurance instrument.
points.zh: 语调传递的信息不亚于内容：用『你受伤时真正在乎你的人』的那种平稳、安定的声音说话——声音本身就是一件安抚的器械。

points.en: Always respond to what a patient says — receiving no answer at all is about the most insulting thing a provider can do. Not ready with a definitive reply? Nod or restate what they said, and come back with more information once you have it.
points.zh: 患者说的每句话都要有回应——问了、说了却得不到任何回音，几乎是医疗人员能给出的最大侮辱。暂时给不出确定答复？点头或复述他的话就行，等有了更多信息再补上。

points.en: Introduce yourself with full name and profession — 'I'm a paramedic' — because the patient is entrusting privacy and medical well-being to a stranger and deserves to know what you know and what you do not. The introduction also declares: whatever the indignities of treatment, you remain in charge of your own health care, and we speak as equals.
points.zh: 自我介绍要报全名加职业——『我是救护员』——因为患者正把隐私和健康托付给一分钟前还是陌生人的你，他有权知道你懂什么、不懂什么。这句介绍还是一份声明：无论治疗多么有失体面，主导你健康照护的仍是你自己，我们平等对话。

points.en: Open with the name, not the complaint: 'Hi, my name is …, I'm a paramedic. What's your name?' beats 'What's the problem?'. Then honour the formality the patient chooses — if they say call me Joey, do; if they say I am Mr. Jones, never downgrade to Joey or buddy.
points.zh: 开场问名字，不问病情：『你好，我叫某某，是救护员。您怎么称呼？』远胜『哪里不舒服？』。之后尊重患者自选的称呼级别——人家说叫我 Joey 就叫 Joey；人家说我是 Jones 先生，就绝不能降格叫小名或『哥们儿』。

points.en: The name question doubles as a mini mental status examination: to answer, the patient must hear you, locate your voice and meet your gaze, process the meaning, formulate an accurate response from memory, and speak it coherently — all within about 1 second. Close enough to see pupil size, that single exchange screens mental state and at least six pairs of cranial nerves.
points.zh: 问名字同时就是一次微型精神状态检查：要答上来，患者得听见你的话、定位声源并与你对视、理解语义、从记忆里组织出准确回答、再连贯地说出口——全程约1秒完成。若你近得能看清瞳孔，这一问一答已经筛查了精神状态和至少六对脑神经。

points.en: Assume fear is on scene: most patients are scared to death, and when the patient is not, a loved one may be terrified instead. Reassurance ranks among the most important treatments you carry. Fear is controlled three ways — your visible competence and professional calm, honest caring (which people detect as easily as kindness), and giving information.
points.zh: 默认现场一定有恐惧：多数患者怕得要命；患者不怕的时候，往往是家属吓坏了。安抚是你携带的最重要『药物』之一。控制恐惧靠三招——看得见的专业沉稳、发自内心的在乎（这一点旁人一测一个准）、以及给信息。

points.en: Giving information means treating the patient as an adult: say what you think is happening, show them the ECG, tell them their blood pressure, explain the plan and their progress. Nothing harnesses the patient's own self-healing power — and the healing power of loved ones — better, while stabilizing everyone's emotions.
points.zh: 『给信息』就是把患者当成年人对待：说出你判断发生了什么，把心电图给他看，报出血压，讲清你打算怎么处理、他现在情况如何。没有比这更能调动患者自愈力量和亲人支持力量的方法，同时所有人的情绪都被稳住了。

points.en: Pain doctrine: when someone reports pain, acknowledge that you grasp it — then do something about it, with a medical consultation if necessary. Ignoring pain is called one of the most grievous offenses by health care providers; no patient should ever have to tolerate pain you can alleviate.
points.zh: 疼痛的铁律：患者说疼，先让他知道你听懂了、当回事——然后就要行动，必要时连线医疗指导。无视疼痛被原书列为医疗人员最严重的过失之一；凡是你有能力缓解的疼痛，患者一秒都不该被要求忍。

points.en: Modesty matters no matter how acute the condition — most of all to the very old, adolescents, and sometimes the very young; and when an impaired patient cannot feel the exposure, the family certainly does. Cover with a blanket or towel and treat the patient as you would want your own loved ones treated.
points.zh: 再急的病也不能不顾体面——最在意的是高龄老人、青少年，有时还有幼儿；患者因意识受损感觉不到暴露时，家属可全都看在眼里。用毯子或毛巾遮盖，用你希望别人对待你家人的方式对待患者。

points.en: Help, do not judge: addicts commonly lie to protect their addiction — few will admit past two beers, let alone opiates — yet you still need the truth to treat (naloxone for the opiate user). Your moral code takes a back seat to professional ethics; causes of addiction are complex, and providers see only the results of people's choices.
points.zh: 帮忙，别审判：成瘾者常靠说谎护住毒瘾——肯承认喝超过两瓶啤酒的都少，更别说承认用了阿片——但治疗恰恰需要真话（阿片使用者要用纳洛酮）。你的个人道德观必须给职业伦理让座；成瘾成因复杂，医疗人员看到的只是选择的结果。

points.en: Lie-detection heuristic: a plain, simple question answered with an unnecessarily complicated or inappropriate response should raise the possibility of lying — but also of mental impairment from chemicals, hypoxia, or psychiatric disorder. Either way, do not appoint yourself judge: label the patient a poor historian and move on. Professional skepticism aids clinical decisions; cynicism is skepticism gone wild and helps no one.
points.zh: 识谎的经验法则：用平实的语言问了个简单问题，得到的却是没必要的绕弯或牛头不对马嘴的回答——要想到说谎的可能，也要想到化学物质、缺氧或精神疾病造成的思维紊乱。无论哪种，都别自封法官：把他标记为『病史叙述不可靠』，继续问诊。职业性怀疑帮助临床决策；犬儒是怀疑的脱缰版，对谁都没好处。

sections.titleEn: Conducting the Interview: Three Question Types, Six Rescue Tools
sections.titleZh: 问诊进行时：三类提问，六件救场工具

points.en: Open-ended questions make the patient do the thinking: no yes/no answer, no menu of options. Asking about chest pain, do NOT offer 'sharp, dull, pressure' — the patient's own word describes the feeling more accurately. Stock examples: How have you been feeling lately? What do you think is causing this? What other health concerns do you have?
points.zh: 开放式提问让患者自己动脑：答案不是是/否，也不给选项菜单。问胸痛时，『刺痛、钝痛、压榨感』这些词不能替他说出口——患者自己想出的那个词才最贴近真实感受。常备句式：最近感觉怎么样？你觉得是什么引起的？还有哪些健康上的担心？

points.en: Closed-ended (direct) questions fetch specifics — ideal for medical history. Build a standard set asked of nearly every patient, in plain words, never talking down and never in medical jargon: heart problems, lung problems, high or low blood pressure, diabetes, seizures, fainting spells, prior head injury, and whether they have both lungs and both kidneys.
points.zh: 封闭式（直接）提问抓具体事实——最适合查病史。准备一套几乎每个患者都要过一遍的标准问题，用大白话问、不居高临下也不甩医学术语：心脏病史？肺部问题？血压高或低？糖尿病？癫痫？晕厥史？头部受过伤吗？两肺两肾都在吗？

points.en: For a woman of childbearing age — generally 12 to 50 years — the closed-ended set extends, when applicable, to pregnancies, deliveries and abortions, the last menstrual period and whether it was normal, and any gynecologic surgeries.
points.zh: 面对育龄女性——一般指12～50岁——封闭式问题清单在适用时要加问：怀孕、分娩和流产史，末次月经时间及是否正常，以及做过哪些妇科手术。

points.en: Payoff questions are icebergs: tiny questions exposing huge subsurface issues, sometimes the hidden real reason for the call. The repertoire: Have you ever felt like this before? Have you been upset about anything lately? Are you afraid of someone (saved for the privacy of the ambulance)? Have you been thinking about hurting yourself? What happened the last time you felt this way?
points.zh: 高回报问题是冰山：小小一句，撬出水面下的大问题，有时那才是这通呼叫的真正原因。保留曲目：以前有过这种感觉吗？最近有什么烦心事吗？你在怕某个人吗（这句留到救护车里私下问）？有没有想过伤害自己？上次这样时后来怎么样了？

points.en: Six strategies rescue an interview when a terrified patient cannot organize their thoughts: facilitate ('Please say more'), be quiet (a few seconds of deliberate silence while they find words), clarify (ask what they mean — it proves you listen), redirect (politely steer back to the dodged question, several times if needed), interpret (vocalize your understanding and invite correction), and simplify-and-summarize (restate a confused answer in simpler terms and check agreement).
points.zh: 当吓坏的患者语无伦次时，有六招能救回问诊：促谈（『请多说一点』）、留白（故意沉默几秒，让他把话找出来）、澄清（请他解释所指——这本身就证明你在听）、拉回（礼貌地把话题引回被回避的问题，必要时多引几次）、试解（说出你的理解，请他纠正）、化简归纳（把混乱的回答换成更简单的话复述，问他同不同意）。

points.en: The simplify-and-summarize tool is built for the hardest communicators — patients with psychiatric problems, patients who fabricate illness, and those too afraid or upset to speak plainly: your simpler synopsis helps them focus and helps you interview.
points.zh: 『化简归纳』正是为最难沟通的对象准备的——有精神疾病的、伪造病情的、吓懵或情绪崩溃到说不清话的患者：你给出的简化版摘要既帮他聚拢思路，也帮你把问诊推进下去。

points.en: Garbage in, garbage out applies to interviews: careless questions produce useless answers. And if an urgent task forces you to stop a patient from talking, explain why they need to be quiet and promise the conversation resumes when the task is done.
points.zh: 『输入垃圾，输出垃圾』同样适用于问诊：问题问得草率，答案就没法用。若紧急操作迫使你打断患者说话，要解释清楚为什么此刻需要安静，并承诺操作一完就继续听他讲。

sections.titleEn: Common Interviewing Errors: Six Named Traps
sections.titleZh: 问诊常见错误：六个有名有姓的坑

points.en: Making assumptions is the parent of most provider mistakes — the textbook's own examples: assuming a patient is faking unconsciousness or seizures, assuming a companion is a spouse, assuming a fight victim belongs to a gang, assuming a patient is inebriated. The antidote is careful observation with an open mind.
points.zh: 『想当然』是医疗人员大多数错误的源头——教材亲自点的例子：认定患者在装昏迷或装抽搐、认定陪同者是配偶、认定斗殴伤者是帮派成员、认定患者是喝多了。解药是仔细观察、脑子对各种可能性敞开。

points.en: Giving medical advice: being consulted like a physician is an honour that conveys trust, but the correct move — including when asked to comment on a physician's decision — is to suggest they obtain medical advice from a doctor.
points.zh: 替人拿医疗主意：被当成医生来咨询是一种信任的荣誉，但正确动作——包括被请去评价某位医生的决定时——是建议他们向医生获取医疗意见。

points.en: False hope has a scripted alternative: to a stable-looking patient asking 'Am I going to die?', answer along the lines of 'Some day — but you look pretty good to us today', or 'I don't know, but I sure hope not — what do you think?'. To the same question about an unstable patient: 'We think he is very sick, but we're doing everything we possibly can to help.'
points.zh: 不给虚假希望，但有现成话术：状态尚稳的患者问『我会死吗？』，可以答『总有一天会——但今天在我们看来你气色不错』，或『我不知道，但我真心希望不会——你自己觉得呢？』。若患者情况不稳，家属或本人再问，就答『我们认为他病得很重，但我们正在尽一切可能帮他』。

points.en: The statement 'I think I'm going to die' is categorically different from the question 'Am I going to die?': patients who look you in the eye and declare it are probably right — cardiogenic shock and end-stage COPD patients do this with uncanny regularity. The response is not debate but action: invite the family to kiss the patient before transport; it may be the last chance, and they will treasure it forever.
points.zh: 陈述句『我觉得我要死了』和疑问句『我会死吗？』是两码事：直视你的眼睛说出前者的患者，多半是对的——心源性休克和终末期慢阻肺患者说这话准得出奇。回应不是辩论而是行动：转运前请家属亲吻患者道别；那可能是最后的机会，这个记忆他们会珍藏一生。

points.en: Assuming excessive authority: paramedics are not police officers, and adopting a law officer's no-nonsense demeanour frightens the patient and makes caring for them nearly impossible.
points.zh: 摆过头的权威：救护员不是警察，端出执法者那副不容分说的做派会吓到患者，让照护工作几乎无法进行。

points.en: Sidestepping the truth: the blood pressure, the ECG findings, the glucose reading, and your presumptive diagnosis are not secrets to keep from the patient. Remind them you are not a physician and hold no definitive answers — then say what you think is going on, honestly and sincerely, never harshly.
points.zh: 绕开真相：血压值、心电图结果、血糖读数、你的拟诊断，都不是要瞒着患者的机密。先说明你不是医生、给不了定论——然后把你的判断讲出来，诚恳坦率，但绝不刻薄。

points.en: Professional distancing — dodging contact with patients as people via jargon they will not understand and half-truth answers — is a described Western-medicine habit the chapter tells you NOT to adopt: it serves neither your well-being nor the patient's in the long run.
points.zh: 职业疏离——用患者听不懂的术语、用半真半假的回答，来回避与患者的『人对人』接触——是教材描述过、并明令你不要学的西医积习：长远看，对你和患者的身心都没有半点好处。

sections.titleEn: Nonverbal Skills: What Your Body Says Before You Do
sections.titleZh: 非语言技巧：你还没开口，身体已经说了

points.en: Eye contact flips meaning across species: animals read direct eye contact as aggression, but people expect brief, frequent, direct eye contact — especially when they need reassurance. Meeting a patient's eyes communicates honesty and concern, and the text calls it a baseline necessity of sincere communication.
points.zh: 目光接触的含义在物种间正好翻转：动物把直视当挑衅，人却期待短暂而频繁的直接对视——尤其在需要安抚的时候。与患者对视传递的是诚实与关切，原书称之为一切真诚沟通的底线配置。

points.en: Busy hands steal eye contact: when the patient's condition is subacute, task-absorption correlates with less or no eye contact. If the patient needs someone to talk to, deliberately take the time to listen when you can.
points.zh: 手一忙，眼神就丢了：患者情况亚急性时，埋头操作往往对应着目光接触变少甚至归零。患者需要有人说话时，要刻意腾出时间去听。

points.en: Touch is a test-first tool: gently touch a neutral body part — shoulder or arm — when reassuring or easing fear, then read the reaction. Pulling away means touch will not be a valuable strategy here; leaning in or relaxing means it will work. Gentleness extends touch to the untouchable: it lives in how you seat the stethoscope, wrap the cuff, or lay the blanket.
points.zh: 触碰是一件『先试探再使用』的工具：安抚时轻触中性部位——肩膀或手臂——然后读反应。对方缩回去，说明触碰在这个人身上行不通；身体前倾或放松下来，就说明有效。而『轻柔』能把触碰延伸到不愿被碰的人身上：它藏在你贴听诊器、缠血压袖带、盖毯子的手法里。

points.en: Posture rules for the terrified patient: never stand over them with arms folded — that is confrontation, not concern. Position yourself at or below their eye level, sitting, kneeling, or squatting at an angle that stays out of their personal space; paramedics squat before patients seated in cars or on benches, or sit on the drug box.
points.zh: 面对吓坏的患者的站位规则：绝不能抱臂立在人家面前——那是对峙，不是关心。把自己放到与对方视线齐平或更低的位置，坐、跪或蹲，角度上避开他的私人空间；很多救护员会在坐在车里、长椅或沙发上的患者面前蹲下，或干脆坐在药箱上。

points.en: Demeanour and the therapeutic smile: people in crisis must read you as safe to be with, nonthreatening, and honestly caring — from that follows their belief that you will handle the crisis. A smile is a proven stress reliever; the same smile that once told you everything would be OK is now yours to give.
points.zh: 风度与治疗性微笑：危机中的人必须从你身上读出『这人待着安全、没有威胁、真心在乎我』——由此才会相信你能搞定这场危机。微笑是被验证过的减压器；当年那个让你相信『一切都会好』的微笑，如今轮到你来给出。

sections.titleZh: 在对话里完成精神状态评估

points.en: Spontaneous appropriate humour is called the highest form of mental function: producing it demands high cognitive function plus an intact memory, and a patient not thinking clearly has no neuronal reserve to spend on wit. A well-timed joke from the patient is a reassuring finding.
points.zh: 自发且得体的幽默被称为心智功能的最高形态：造一个恰到好处的玩笑需要高级认知功能加完整的记忆，脑子不清楚的人根本匀不出神经元来搞幽默。患者能适时开个玩笑，本身就是个让人放心的发现。

points.en: Response timing is a measurable sign: a clearly thinking patient answers simple, sensible questions within 1 second. Longer latency to easy questions is data, not rudeness.
points.zh: 应答速度是可测量的体征：思维清楚的患者对简单合理的问题应在1秒内答上来。简单问题答得慢，是临床数据，不是没礼貌。

points.en: Orientation is memory in four items — person (who they are and who you are), place, day of the week, and event (what happened that got you called). An incorrect answer to any of the four constitutes memory dysfunction and possibly decreased blood flow to the brain.
points.zh: 定向力就是四项记忆——人（他是谁、你是谁）、地点、星期几、事件（发生了什么才叫的救护车）。四项中任何一项答错都构成记忆功能障碍，并提示脑血流可能下降。

points.en: Failure to obey simple commands localizes: any disruption in complying with the preceding steps indicates dysfunction in the cerebrum or possibly the cerebellum — which may be acute or a preexisting condition. Establish the patient's baseline before calling it new.
points.zh: 听不懂简单指令能定位病灶：前述任一环节的配合出现中断，提示大脑或小脑功能障碍——可能是急性的，也可能是原有的。先弄清患者的基线，再判断是不是新发。

sections.titleEn: Special Interview Situations: Silent, Hostile, Very Old, Very Young
sections.titleZh: 特殊问诊情境：不说话的、带敌意的、很老的、很小的

points.en: The patient unmotivated to talk: if there are no signs of altered mental status, do not force the issue. Keep eye contact, express concern every way you can, explain everything you are doing, invite them repeatedly to answer, and tell them it is all right not to talk — accepting them as they are is what breaks the barrier down.
points.zh: 不想说话的患者：只要没有意识状态改变的迹象，就不必硬撬。保持目光接触，用一切方式表达关切，解释你做的每一步，反复邀请他回答，并明说不想讲也没关系——接纳他本来的样子，恰恰是拆墙最快的方法。

points.en: The hostile patient: insults from people in crisis are guaranteed and frequent, most predictably from the chemically impaired. Never respond in kind — nothing escalates faster than trading insults, witnesses are usually plentiful, and you are on their turf, where they know everything and you know nothing. Accept that you cannot fix everyone emotionally: if the scene slips out of control, defer to police.
points.zh: 带敌意的患者：来自危机中人群的辱骂是必然且频繁的，神志被化学物质搅浑的人尤其可以预料。绝不回嘴——没有什么比对骂升级得更快，现场通常不缺目击者，而且你身处对方的地盘：他了如指掌，你两眼一抹黑。接受『情绪不是人人能修』的现实：局面失控就交给警察。

points.en: Older patients are not presumed harder to talk to — what is genuinely different is complexity: more than one disease at a time and more concurrent medications, plus individual variation in hearing, eyesight, mental status, and mobility that you adapt to case by case.
points.zh: 老年患者不能预设『难沟通』——真正不同的是复杂度：常常几种病并存、多种药同服，听力、视力、精神状态和行动力又人人不同，你要逐例适配。

points.en: Children in one profile: they protest pain vigorously, fear strangers, panic when separated from parents, and their bodies are less familiar to many providers. Early in the contact, equipment matters less than friendly eye contact, smiles, and calm, subdued, age-matched explanations — minimize your movements, lower your voice, touch as gently as you can, and get to or below the child's eye level.
points.zh: 儿童患者的一张画像：喊疼喊得惊天动地、怕生人、一离开父母就恐慌，而且很多急救者对小身体的解剖远不如对成人熟悉。接触初期，器械远不如友善的对视、微笑和平静低缓、按年龄定制的解释重要——动作放小、音量放低、触碰放轻，把自己降到孩子视线的高度或更低。

points.en: Parent involvement scales inversely with age: for a conscious small child, hands-on parental help (holding an extremity during IV insertion) matters most with infants and toddlers and much less with older children. No parent available? Toys bridge the gap — crews stock teddy bears, and an examination glove inflated with eyes drawn in felt marker becomes a serviceable chicken; make it in front of the child, not offstage.
points.zh: 家长参与度和孩子年龄成反比：清醒的小患者让家长上手帮忙（打静脉时扶住肢体），对婴幼儿最有用，对大孩子作用就小得多。家长不在场？玩具来搭桥——不少车组常备玩具熊；没有的话，把检查手套吹起来、用记号笔点上眼睛，就是一只能用的『小鸡』——要当着孩子的面做，别背着他做好再拿来。

points.en: Adolescents (beginning at age 12) may want no parent present for questioning or examination — and an adult who insists on monitoring the conversation should itself raise questions in your mind. Do not refuse a parent's prerogative, but report the situation to the emergency physician and chart it accurately. Deal with adolescents as adults: offer options, honour their choices, never offer an option you cannot honour, and guard their modesty above all — they are mostly obsessed with image.
points.zh: 青少年（从12岁起）问诊和查体时可能根本不想让父母在场——而一个坚持要旁听谈话的成年人，本身就该在你心里立起问号。家长的权利不能拒绝，但要把情况汇报给急诊医生并如实记录。对青少年要当成人对待：给选项、兑现他的选择、绝不给出你兑现不了的选项，并且格外保护隐私体面——他们大多对形象极度在意。

points.en: Patients with speech, hearing, or sight disorders must not be overlooked: many providers take sign-language or lip-reading classes; family members and primary caregivers who know the patient can both translate and calm fear; hospitals and 9-1-1 communications centres offer interpreter capabilities — and you should know in advance what sign-language resources exist locally.
points.zh: 有言语、听力或视力障碍的患者绝不能被绕过去：不少急救者专门去学手语或唇读；熟悉患者的家属和主要照护者既能当翻译又能安抚恐惧；医院和9-1-1通讯中心备有传译资源——当地有哪些手语支援，你应当事先摸清。

points.en: The touch vocabulary for communication-limited patients: a light touch on the shoulder conveys kindness, a firm grasp expresses reassurance, some respond to a brief one-armed hug, and in some situations you can hold the patient's face between your hands and let your eyes do the calming.
points.zh: 对沟通受限患者的『触碰词汇表』：肩上轻轻一搭传递善意，手上稳稳一握表达安心，有人吃『单臂短暂一抱』这一套，有些情形甚至可以双手捧住患者的脸，用眼神完成安抚。

sections.titleEn: Cross-Cultural Communication: Respect Is the Key Component
sections.titleZh: 跨文化沟通：核心只有一个词——尊重

points.en: The most common communication barriers are listed: race, ethnicity, age, gender, language, education, religion, geography, and economic status — their combination is what defines culture. Everyone carries some prejudice to stay conscious of, and using your own culture as the only reference is likened to imposing your own morality on patients.
points.zh: 最常见的沟通壁垒被一一列出：种族、族裔、年龄、性别、语言、教育、宗教、地域、经济状况——它们的组合就定义了文化。每个人都带着需要自省的偏见；只拿自己的文化当参照系，无异于把自己的道德观强加给患者。

points.en: The professional obligation is homework: research which cultural, ethnic, and religious groups are prevalent in your practice area and learn how to interact with each. You will not get everything right — but the effort itself translates as respect, and respect is named the key component.
points.zh: 职业义务里包含一份功课：查清你执业区域主要有哪些文化、族裔和宗教群体，学习各自的相处之道。你不可能事事做对——但努力本身就会被读成尊重，而尊重正是被点名的核心要素。

points.en: Manners are operational, not decorative: use the patient's name, plus 'Yes sir', 'No ma'am', 'Please', and 'Thank you'; ask 'Would you… / Could you… / May I…' because most people want to grant permission before being touched. Assuming permission is singled out as particularly demeaning to an older nursing-home resident — it silently says they are not important or competent enough to be asked. When involuntary bodily functions erupt mid-exam, a simple 'Excuse me' keeps the embarrassment temporary.
points.zh: 礼貌是操作规范，不是装饰品：称呼患者的名字，『先生』『女士』『请』『谢谢』挂在嘴边；动手前先问『可以吗／方便吗／我能不能』——大多数人都希望被触碰之前先被征求同意。教材特别点名：对养老院的老人假定同意、免去询问，是格外贬低人的——那等于无声地说『你不重要，也没资格被问』。查体中途遇到不由自主的生理状况，一句『不好意思』就能让尴尬只停留一瞬。

points.en: Hand-gesture minefield, straight from the text: the Canadian thumbs-up equals an extended middle finger in many Arabic and some Latin countries; the OK sign (thumb-index circle) references the anus in Latin countries, Germany, Italy, and Russia, means zero or worthless in France, the evil eye in other cultures, and money or coins in Japan; and in Japan the middle finger is merely used for pointing, like an index finger.
points.zh: 手势雷区，原文照录：加拿大人竖大拇指的『没问题』，在许多阿拉伯国家和部分拉美国家等于竖中指；拇指食指圈成的OK手势，在拉美国家、德国、意大利、俄罗斯指肛门，在法国表示零或『不值钱』，在另一些文化里是毒眼诅咒，在日本则表示钱或要硬币；而在日本，中指只是当食指用来指东西的。

points.en: Eye-contact geography: most Asian, African, Latin American, and Caribbean cultures show respect by avoiding direct eye contact — with Somali and Brazilian cultures as named exceptions; in Arab, Somali, and Brazilian cultures, prolonged eye contact is welcomed as communicating honesty and interest.
points.zh: 目光接触的地理学：多数亚洲、非洲、拉美和加勒比文化以回避直视表达尊重——索马里和巴西文化是被点名的例外；在阿拉伯、索马里和巴西文化中，长时间对视反而受欢迎，被视为诚实和关注对方的表现。

points.en: Body-language atlas from the chapter's list: bowing shows rank in Japan (deeper bow, more respect); many Asians avoid having the head touched — it is the body's most sacred part and residence of the soul; Islamic and Hindu cultures avoid the left hand, traditionally reserved for unclean functions; showing the soles of feet or shoes insults in Muslim nations and most of Thailand ('you are beneath my feet'); slouching offends in Japan and Northern Europe; hands in pockets disrespect in Turkey; crossed legs offend in Turkey and Ghana; hands on hips signal hostility in Mexico and Argentina.
points.zh: 肢体语言地图，按原书清单：鞠躬在日本标示身份等级（弯得越深，敬意越重）；许多亚洲人忌讳被摸头——头是全身最神圣的部位、灵魂的居所；伊斯兰与印度教文化避用左手，传统上左手做不洁之事，伸左手致意是无礼冒犯；在穆斯林国家和泰国大部分地区，亮出脚底或鞋底等于说『你不如我脚下的土』；瘫坐没坐相在日本和北欧惹人反感；手插口袋在土耳其失敬；跷二郎腿在土耳其和加纳失礼；双手叉腰在墨西哥和阿根廷是敌意信号。

points.en: The nod is not universal: Indian and Arabic people may signal agreement by moving the head side to side — the Western 'no' — and indicate no by tipping the head back with a click of the tongue. The one gesture that travels everywhere is the smile: received by almost every culture as goodwill and acceptance. Practice it often.
points.zh: 点头摇头并不通用：印度和阿拉伯人群可能用左右摆头表示同意——正是西方的『不』——而用后仰头加舌头弹上颚的咔哒声表示否定。真正走遍天下的手势只有微笑：几乎所有文化都把它接收为善意与接纳。请多多练习。

points.en: The chapter's closing verdict: communicating compassion, care, and understanding matters as much as starting IV lines and other advanced skills — emotional intelligence shapes your relationships with patients, subordinates, peers, and superiors, and without it the paramedic road gets bumpy.
points.zh: 全章收官判词：传递同情、关怀与理解的能力，和打静脉、做高级操作的能力同等重要——情商决定你与患者、下级、同侪、上级的全部关系；缺了它，救护员这条路会颠簸不断。

hardNumbers.itemEn: Share of calls that enter patients' homes
hardNumbers.itemZh: 出勤进入患者家中的比例

hardNumbers.itemEn: Name-question mini mental exam: response window / cranial nerves screened
hardNumbers.itemZh: 问名字＝微型精神检查：应答时限／筛查脑神经
育龄范围（女性需加问妇产史）
青少年期起点（可拒绝家长在场）

hardNumbers.itemEn: Response window for a clearly thinking patient
hardNumbers.itemZh: 思维清楚患者的应答时限

atScene.en: Patients watch how the crew treats each other: mutual respect between paramedics on scene directly raises the patient's confidence in you.
atScene.zh: 患者会观察队友之间怎么相处：现场救护员彼此尊重，患者对你的信任度会直接上升。

atScene.en: Never open with loud, slow speech to an older patient on the assumption they are deaf — plenty are not, and 'I'm not deaf' is a deserved rebuke that costs you the rapport.
atScene.zh: 别一上来就冲老年患者又大声又放慢地说话、默认人家耳背——很多老人听力好得很，一句『我不聋』就是你应得的教训，融洽关系也随之泡汤。

atScene.en: Explain to family members early what is happening and what they can do — information is the treatment for their fear and worry, and calm relatives make a workable scene.
atScene.zh: 尽早告诉家属正在发生什么、他们能做什么——信息就是治他们恐惧和焦虑的药，家属稳了，现场才好开展工作。

atScene.en: No whispering, laughing, or snickering with your partner within a patient's sight or earshot — even when it is not about them, they will feel it is. It reads as unprofessional every single time.
atScene.zh: 在患者看得见、听得到的范围内，不许和搭档咬耳朵、说笑或窃笑——哪怕说的根本不是他，他也会觉得就是在说他。这种举动无一例外显得不专业。

atScene.en: Aggression warning triad: clenched fists, intense staring directed at you, heavy breathing through clenched teeth — read them as rising anger and possible imminent attack.
atScene.zh: 攻击预警三联征：攥紧的拳头、死死盯住你的目光、咬着牙的粗重呼吸——读到它们就是怒气在升级、袭击可能在路上。

atScene.en: An adult who insists on monitoring your conversation with an adolescent is itself a finding: comply with the parental prerogative, but report it to the emergency physician and chart it accurately.
atScene.zh: 一个坚持全程旁听你与青少年谈话的成年人，本身就是一个『发现』：家长的权利照给，但要向急诊医生汇报此事，并如实写进记录。

confusions.en: Closing an open question: asking about chest pain and then offering 'sharp? dull? pressure?' hands the patient your words instead of theirs. A true open-ended question has no yes/no answer and no menu — the patient's own descriptor is the more accurate one.
confusions.zh: 把开放式问题问『闭』了：问胸痛却顺嘴递上『刺痛？钝痛？压榨感？』，等于把你的词塞进患者嘴里。真正的开放式提问没有是/否答案、不给选项菜单——患者自己想出的形容词才最准。

confusions.en: 'No problem' versus 'You are very welcome': the textbook rules the first out — it implies the patient was almost a nuisance. Thanks are answered with a full-hearted 'You are very welcome!'.
confusions.zh: 『没事儿』和『不客气，应该的』不是一回事：教材明确否掉前者——那话外音是『你还不算太麻烦』。对道谢的标准回应是真心实意的『不客气！』。

confusions.en: The question 'Am I going to die?' is answered with calibrated honesty ('Some day — but you look pretty good to us today'); the statement 'I think I'm going to die', delivered eye to eye, is treated as probably true — cardiogenic shock and end-stage COPD patients call it with uncanny regularity. Mixing up the two scripts fails the question.
confusions.zh: 疑问句『我会死吗？』用有分寸的诚实来答（『总有一天——但今天你在我们看来气色不错』）；直视着你说出的陈述句『我觉得我要死了』则按『多半是真的』处理——心源性休克和终末期慢阻肺患者说这话准得出奇。两套话术用反了，这题就错了。

confusions.en: Active listening is not nodding along: it specifically means repeating key parts of the patient's answers (ideally while writing them down). Deliberate silence is a different tool — 'be quiet' — used when the patient is struggling to find words.
confusions.zh: 积极倾听不是一个劲点头：它特指把患者回答的关键内容复述回去（最好边记边复述）。刻意沉默是另一件工具——『留白』——用在患者努力找词却说不出来的时候。

confusions.en: Professional skepticism versus cynicism: skepticism is a tool that sharpens clinical decisions; cynicism is 'skepticism gone wild' — the occupational corrosion that follows from letting yourself judge patients. The chapter's fix for a suspected liar is a label, not a verdict: 'poor historian', then move on.
confusions.zh: 职业性怀疑与犬儒的分界：怀疑是打磨临床判断的工具；犬儒是『脱缰的怀疑』——放任自己审判患者之后必然到来的职业腐蚀。对疑似说谎者，教材给的处理是贴标签而非下判决：记一句『病史叙述不可靠』，继续问诊。

confusions.en: Assuming gestures are universal: the thumbs-up reads as an extended middle finger in many Arabic and some Latin countries, and the OK sign is obscene in Latin countries, Germany, Italy, and Russia. The only gesture that travels everywhere is the smile.
confusions.zh: 以为手势走遍天下都一样：竖大拇指在许多阿拉伯国家和部分拉美国家等于竖中指，OK手势在拉美国家、德国、意大利、俄罗斯是下流话。真正全球通行的手势只有微笑。

confusions.en: Payoff questions are not routine history: they sit outside the standard set ('Are you afraid of someone?', 'Have you been thinking about hurting yourself?') and exist to surface the hidden reason for the call — some are asked only in the privacy of the ambulance.
confusions.zh: 高回报问题不属于常规病史：它们在标准问题清单之外（『你在怕某个人吗？』『有没有想过伤害自己？』），专为钓出这通呼叫背后隐藏的真正原因——有几句只能等到救护车里私下问。

mnemonics.name: 救场六招：促·静·澄·拉·试·简
mnemonics.en: Facilitate ('say more') · be Quiet · Clarify · Redirect · Interpret (say what you think they meant) · Simplify-and-summarize — the six tools for a patient too frightened to organize their thoughts.
mnemonics.zh: 促谈（『请多说点』）· 留白 · 澄清 · 拉回 · 试解（说出你的理解请他纠正）· 化简归纳——患者吓得语无伦次时的六件救场工具，按『促静澄拉试简』一口气背下。

mnemonics.name: 控恐三件套：稳·情·讯
mnemonics.en: Fear is controlled by Steadiness (visible competence and calm), Sincerity (honest caring people can detect), and Sharing information (show the ECG, tell the BP, explain the plan).
mnemonics.zh: 控制恐惧靠三样：稳（看得见的专业沉稳）、情（测得出的真心在乎）、讯（给信息——看心电图、报血压、讲计划）。稳住自己、掏出真心、交出信息。

mnemonics.name: 问名字＝1秒6神经
mnemonics.en: The name question is a stealth exam: hear → locate and meet your gaze → process → recall → speak coherently, all within about 1 second — and with pupils in view you have screened at least six pairs of cranial nerves.
mnemonics.zh: 问名字就是暗中查体：听见→定位声源并对视→理解→从记忆调取→连贯说出，全程约1秒——凑近看清瞳孔的话，至少六对脑神经已经筛完。

selfCheck.qEn: Define the three question types of this chapter and give one example of each.
selfCheck.qZh: 说出本章的三类提问并各举一例。
selfCheck.aEn: Open-ended (no yes/no, no options): 'How have you been feeling lately?'. Closed-ended (specific fact): 'Do you have diabetes?'. Payoff (tiny question, huge subsurface issue): 'Have you been thinking about hurting yourself?'.
selfCheck.aZh: 开放式（无是/否、不给选项）：『最近感觉怎么样？』；封闭式（问具体事实）：『有糖尿病吗？』；高回报（小问题撬大冰山）：『有没有想过伤害自己？』

selfCheck.qEn: What exactly is active listening, and what two things does it accomplish?
selfCheck.qZh: 积极倾听到底是什么动作？它同时做成哪两件事？
selfCheck.aEn: Repeating the key parts of the patient's responses, ideally while taking notes. It convinces the patient you truly want to hear them, and it confirms the information so there is no misunderstanding.
selfCheck.aZh: 把患者回答中的关键内容复述回去，最好同时做记录。一是让患者相信你真想听，二是当场核对信息、杜绝误解。

selfCheck.qEn: Walk through why 'What's your name?' is a mini mental status examination.
selfCheck.qZh: 解释为什么『您怎么称呼？』就是一次微型精神状态检查。
selfCheck.aEn: To answer, the patient must hear the words, locate the voice and meet your gaze, process meaning, formulate an accurate response from memory, and speak coherently — within about 1 second. Close enough to see the pupils, you have also screened at least six pairs of cranial nerves.
selfCheck.aZh: 要答上来，患者得听见、定位声源并与你对视、理解语义、从记忆组织出准确回答、连贯说出——全程约1秒。近得能看清瞳孔的话，至少六对脑神经也一并筛过了。

selfCheck.qEn: A patient in obvious distress looks you in the eye and says 'I think I'm going to die.' What do you know, and what do you do?
selfCheck.qZh: 一名明显不适的患者直视你说『我觉得我要死了』。你知道什么？该做什么？
selfCheck.aEn: Such patients are probably right — cardiogenic shock and end-stage COPD patients say it with uncanny regularity. Do not argue it away: invite family members to kiss the patient before transport; it may be their last chance and they will treasure the memory.
selfCheck.aZh: 这种患者多半是对的——心源性休克和终末期慢阻肺患者说这话准得出奇。别急着否认安慰：转运前请家属亲吻患者道别；那可能是最后的机会，这份记忆他们会珍藏一生。

selfCheck.qEn: Name the six common interviewing errors.
selfCheck.qZh: 说出六种常见的问诊错误。
selfCheck.aEn: Making assumptions; giving medical advice; providing false hope; assuming excessive authority (playing police officer); sidestepping the truth; and professional distancing (jargon and half-truths to avoid contact with patients as people).
selfCheck.aZh: 想当然；替人拿医疗主意；给虚假希望；摆过头的权威（扮警察）；绕开真相；职业疏离（用术语和半真半假的话回避与患者的人际接触）。

selfCheck.qEn: In which cultures is avoiding direct eye contact a sign of respect — and where is prolonged eye contact welcomed?
selfCheck.qZh: 哪些文化把回避直视当作尊重？哪些文化欢迎长时间对视？
selfCheck.aEn: Most Asian, African, Latin American, and Caribbean cultures avoid direct eye contact out of respect (Somali and Brazilian cultures are exceptions); Arab, Somali, and Brazilian cultures welcome prolonged eye contact as honesty and interest.
selfCheck.aZh: 多数亚洲、非洲、拉美和加勒比文化以回避直视示敬（索马里和巴西文化除外）；阿拉伯、索马里和巴西文化欢迎长时间对视，视之为诚实与关注。

selfCheck.qEn: Orientation testing covers which four memory items, and what does any wrong answer mean?
selfCheck.qZh: 定向力测试查哪四项记忆？任何一项答错意味着什么？
selfCheck.aEn: Person (who they are and who you are), place, day of the week, and event (why you were called). Any incorrect response constitutes memory dysfunction and possibly decreased blood flow to the brain.
selfCheck.aZh: 人（他是谁、你是谁）、地点、星期几、事件（为什么叫救护车）。任何一项答错都构成记忆功能障碍，提示脑血流可能下降。

bcAlerts.topicEn: Communication is a scored deduction category on the BC practical exam
bcAlerts.topicZh: 沟通在 BC 实操考中是明码标价的扣分项
bcAlerts.bookEn: The textbook frames communication as professional art: rapport, therapeutic listening, family care — with no marks attached.
bcAlerts.bookZh: 教材把沟通当作职业艺术来讲：融洽关系、治疗性倾听、照顾家属——不涉及分数。
bcAlerts.bcEn: BC's simulation grading makes it arithmetic, under Overall Call Management with 25%/15%/10% deduction tiers: failing to communicate with patient, partner, or bystander when it would have benefitted care sits in the heaviest tier; little to no communication is a moderate (15%) deficiency; neglecting to inform the patient of one or two procedures, or minor communication errors, costs 10%. Evaluators explicitly weigh teamwork, delegation, use of witnesses/bystanders, and communication with other health care providers.
bcAlerts.bcZh: BC 的模拟站评分把它算成数学题，归在『整体呼叫管理』下，扣分分 25%/15%/10% 三档：该沟通而未与患者、搭档或旁观者沟通、损及照护的，落在最重一档；几乎不沟通属中度缺陷（15%）；做操作前漏告知患者一两项、或有轻微沟通失误，扣 10%。评分员还明确要看团队协作、任务分派、对目击者/旁观者的利用，以及与其他医疗人员的沟通。
bcAlerts.ref: EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria — Overall Call Management
